items.question: Why does wine bathing liberate the seeker?
premises: In wine bathing the best practitioner seeking liberation becomes kevalī.
Wine is of the nature of Śiva.
All mantras arise from Śiva.
items.inference: Because wine and mantras share Śiva-nature, wine bathing can bring the qualified seeker to liberation.
uncertainties: kevalībhavet may indicate isolated liberation or a specific ritual state.
items.plain_english: In the wine bath, the foremost practitioner who seeks liberation may become liberated, because wine is of the nature of Śiva and all mantras arise from Śiva.

items.question: How is wine shown to be Śiva-natured?
premises: There is no difference between Śiva and Śakti.
The rays arise from Śakti.
Wine produces the bliss of those rays.
items.inference: Since Śakti is non-different from Śiva and wine generates the bliss of Śakti's rays, wine is of the nature of Śiva.
uncertainties: marīcayaḥ may refer to mantra-rays or sensory radiances.
items.plain_english: There is no difference between Śiva and Śakti; the rays arise from Śakti, and wine produces their bliss. Therefore wine is of the nature of Śiva.

rows.grounds: bathing divided by mantra, meditation, absorption

items.question: What counts as true bathing in awakened consciousness?
premises: When the full form of consciousness is awakened, one is fit for ritual action.
Bathing is distinguished as mantra, meditation, and absorption.
What lacks that awakened fullness is not true bathing.
items.inference: True bathing depends on awakened, full consciousness and takes the forms of mantra, meditation, and absorption.
uncertainties: The syntax of the final clause is compressed and allows slight variation in emphasis.
items.plain_english: When the full form of consciousness is awakened, one is fit for ritual action. Bathing distinguished by mantra, meditation, and absorption is real bathing; what lacks that is not.

items.question: Why is bathing considered fitting before ritual acts?
premises: Bathing is fitting because it produces fitness for nyāsa and related rites.
This set of eight baths exists in two modes.
The two modes are outer and inner.
items.inference: Bathing is preparatory for ritual because the eightfold bath operates both externally and internally to establish fitness.
items.plain_english: Bathing is fitting because it brings fitness for nyāsa and other rites. This eightfold bathing is twofold, as outer and inner.

rows.grounds: inundation by nectar from the upper moon
a finger and a half above

items.question: What constitutes the inner form of bathing?
premises: The inner bath is a flooding by the nectar-stream of the upper moon.
This occurs above the cranial aperture.
It pervades a span of one and a half finger-widths and remains established there.
items.inference: Inner bathing is an internal inundation by lunar nectar localized above the cranial aperture.
uncertainties: The exact anatomical referent of randhra is assumed to be the cranial aperture.
items.plain_english: The inner bath is the flooding of nectar from the upper moon, established above the cranial aperture and pervading a span of one and a half finger-widths.

rows.grounds: perform in two, three, or more ways

items.question: How may the inner bathing forms be practiced?
premises: Eight forms are taught, each proceeding from the dvādaśānta.
One may perform any one of these baths.
One may also perform them in two, three, or more modes.
items.inference: The inner bath can be practiced flexibly using one or several of the eight forms arising from the dvādaśānta.
uncertainties: dvitryādiśaḥ may refer to directions, modes, or counts; translated as modes.
items.plain_english: Eight forms are taught, each arising from the dvādaśānta. One may perform any one of these baths, or do them in two, three, or more ways.

rows.grounds: what is to be done after bathing is now instructed

items.question: What follows after the bathing procedure is completed?
premises: The rule of bathing has been declared by Bhairava for purification.
The bathing section is now concluded.
The next duty after bathing is about to be taught.
items.inference: With purification by bathing complete, the text moves to the next ritual duty.
items.plain_english: Thus the rule of bathing has been declared by Bhairava for purification. Now what must be done after bathing is taught.

rows.grounds: proceed to the place of worship
mountain peak, riverbank, solitary liṅga, etc.

items.question: Where should the practitioner go after bathing?
premises: After bathing one should observe that the inner state is clear.
Then one should go to the place of worship.
Such places are described as mountain tops, riverbanks, solitary liṅgas, and the like.
items.inference: With a serene inner state, the practitioner proceeds to a suitable place of worship, whether external or exemplary.
items.plain_english: Seeing that one's inner state is clear, one should then go to the place of worship, such as a mountain top, a riverbank, a solitary liṅga, and so on.

rows.grounds: that is external in this context

items.question: What distinguishes outer and inner sacred places in purpose?
premises: The external places named here serve particular attainments, not liberation.
The inner mountain-top and such are located within the body.
The inner practice involves the application of prāṇa.
items.inference: Outer sacred sites are for specific siddhis, while the inner bodily sites, worked through prāṇa, belong to a different aim.
items.plain_english: Those outer places are for particular attainments, not for liberation. The inner mountain-top and the like are within the body, approached through the application of prāṇa.

items.question: Which sacred locus is always fit for worship?
premises: For practitioners, that method serves attainment but not liberation.
The pīṭha-place is always fit for worship.
This is declared in the scriptures.
items.inference: Unlike outer methods aimed at siddhi, the pīṭha is the scripturally sanctioned locus always suitable for worship.
items.plain_english: For practitioners this is a means to attainment, not to liberation. The pīṭha-place, however, is always fit for worship, as the scriptures declare.

rows.grounds: from outer-inner nature, outside and in the body

items.question: On what authority is the pīṭha said to be outer and inner?
premises: The pīṭha has an outer and inner form.
It is present clearly outside and in the body.
The Supreme Lord set this forth in the Naiśa Sañcāra.
items.inference: The dual outer-inner status of the pīṭha rests on the teaching of the Naiśa Sañcāra.
uncertainties: The exact title form Naiśa Sañcāra is kept as a textual reference.
items.plain_english: That pīṭha, in its outer and inner form, is clearly present outside and in the body, because the Supreme Lord set it forth in the revered Naiśa Sañcāra.

rows.grounds: is the pair bindu and nāda

items.question: What is the foundational pīṭha and what follows from it?
premises: The Lord's will is the supporting pīṭha in which the moving and unmoving world stands.
That foremost pīṭha is Kāmarūpa.
From it arises the pair of bindu and nāda.
items.inference: The cosmic base is the Lord's will as Kāmarūpa, from which the bindu-nāda pair proceeds.
items.plain_english: His will is the supporting pīṭha in which all that moves and does not move is situated. That foremost pīṭha is Kāmarūpa, and from it comes the pair of bindu and nāda.

items.question: How are the first three pīṭhas identified?
premises: The nāda-pīṭha is Pūrṇagiri on the right.
On the left is the pīṭha Uḍḍayana.
Bindu is the chief, and together these form the three pīṭhas.
items.inference: The primary triad of pīṭhas consists of bindu as chief with Pūrṇagiri and Uḍḍayana as its nāda-related seats.
uncertainties: The directional mapping of right and left may be ritual or bodily.
items.plain_english: The nāda-pīṭha is Pūrṇagiri on the right, and on the left is the pīṭha Uḍḍayana. With bindu as the chief, this is the triad of pīṭhas.

items.question: What are the half-pīṭha and the three upapīṭhas?
premises: The half-pīṭha is to be known as having the form of saṃkalpanā.
Beyond that comes the śākta level.
Kuṇḍalinī and Vedakala form the triad of upapīṭhas.
items.inference: After the primary triad, the system recognizes a conceptual half-pīṭha and a śākta triad of upapīṭhas.
uncertainties: The exact grouping of the three upapīṭhas is compressed in the verse.
items.plain_english: One should know the half-pīṭha as having the form of conceptualization. Beyond that, in the śākta domain, Kuṇḍalinī and Vedakala belong to the triad of upapīṭhas.

items.question: Which places form the triad of saṃdohakas?
premises: Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī are two, and Kulagiri is another.
Lālana, Baindava, and Vyāpti are named as a triad.
Together these constitute the three saṃdohakas.
items.inference: The saṃdohaka triad is identified through these named seats and groupings.
uncertainties: The mapping between the named places and the three saṃdohakas is terse and may follow a technical tradition.
items.plain_english: Devīkoṭṭa and Ujjayinī are two, and Kulagiri is another; Lālana, Baindava, and Vyāpti form the triad of saṃdohakas.

items.question: How is the ninefold pīṭha system summarized?
premises: Puṇḍravardhana, Vārendra, and Ekāmra are named in the outer set.
The pīṭha is declared ninefold.
This ninefold division follows an inner-outer sequence.
items.inference: The pīṭha doctrine is organized as a ninefold structure spanning inner and outer correspondences.
items.plain_english: With Puṇḍravardhana, Vārendra, and likewise Ekāmra on the outside, the pīṭha is declared ninefold in an inner-outer sequence.

rows.grounds: the eight petals of the heart-lotus

items.question: How are the eight kṣetras correlated with the body?
premises: Knowers of the kṣetras speak of an eightfold group.
This group corresponds to the eight petals of the heart-lotus.
Prayāga, Varaṇā, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantikā are among them.
items.inference: The eight outer kṣetras are mapped onto the eight petals of the heart-lotus.
uncertainties: Only four of the eight kṣetras are named in this verse.
items.plain_english: Those who know the kṣetras speak of an eightfold group corresponding to the eight petals of the heart-lotus: Prayāga, Varaṇā, then Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantikā.

rows.grounds: they call it the eight front petals of the heart-lotus

items.question: How are the upakṣetras located in the subtle body?
premises: Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and Lāhulā are named among the upakṣetras.
The upakṣetras form an eightfold group.
They are said to correspond to the eight front petals of the heart-lotus.
items.inference: The eight upakṣetras are mapped onto the front petals of the heart-lotus.
uncertainties: Only four upakṣetras are named in this verse.
items.plain_english: Vārāṇasī, Kāliṅga, Kulūtā, and likewise Lāhulā belong to the eight upakṣetras, which they say correspond to the eight front petals of the heart-lotus.

items.question: Which sites complete the upakṣetra set in both registers?
premises: Viraja, Airuḍikā, Hālā, Elā, Pūḥ, Kṣīrikā, Purī, Māyā, and Marudeśa are named.
These belong to the same sacred mapping.
They are understood in both outer and inner form.
items.inference: The upakṣetra series is completed by these names and maintained across external and internal registers.
uncertainties: The exact count alignment with the previous verse follows the traditional list.
items.plain_english: Viraja and Airuḍikā, Hālā, Elā, Pūḥ, Kṣīrikā, Purī, the place called Māyā, and Marudeśa are understood in both outer and inner form.

rows.grounds: the eight upasaṃdohakas at the junctions of heart-lotus petals

items.question: Where are the upasaṃdohakas located and which are named?
premises: The upasaṃdohakas are eight in number.
They correspond to the junctions of the heart-lotus petals.
Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara are named among them.
items.inference: The upasaṃdohakas form an eightfold set mapped to the petal junctions of the heart-lotus.
uncertainties: Only five names appear in this verse; the rest continue in the next.
items.plain_english: The eight upasaṃdohakas correspond to the junctions of the heart-lotus petals: Jālandhara, Naipāla, Kaśmīra, Gargikā, and Hara.

rows.grounds: located at the gate of the mleccha direction
a three-path junction from the meeting of two

items.question: How do the path-junctions arise in this mapping?
premises: Kurukṣetra and Kheṭaka are named, including a site at the mleccha direction gate.
A two-path junction is identified.
A three-path junction arises from the meeting of two, and further junctions from the meeting of three.
items.inference: The sacred map extends from named sites to junctions generated by the convergence of paths.
uncertainties: The phrase mlecchadigdvāravṛttiḥ is technical and may indicate a specific directional station.
items.plain_english: There is also the site at the gate of the mleccha direction, Kurukṣetra, and Kheṭaka. A two-path junction arises, a three-path junction from the meeting of two, and further from the meeting of three.

rows.grounds: ending at nose, palate, and aperture in this body

items.question: How is the four-path junction located in the body?
premises: A four-path junction is recognized through dissolution in the Śakti-bearing principle.
This is held to occur right there.
In the body it is established at the region ending in nose, palate, and aperture.
items.inference: The four-path junction is both a subtle dissolution point and a bodily locus in the upper channels.
uncertainties: The exact anatomical mapping of nāsānta-tālu-randhra is interpretive.
items.plain_english: They hold that the four-path junction arises there itself by dissolution in the Śakti-bearing principle, and in this body it is established in the region of the nose, palate, and aperture.

rows.grounds: called the middle of brows, throat, and heart
the navel, bulb, and abode of great bliss

items.question: Which bodily triads are identified as middle and kaula?
premises: The middle triad is named as the middle of the brows, the throat, and the heart.
Another triad is the navel, the bulb, and the abode of great bliss.
That second triad is called kaula.
items.inference: The text maps sacred structure onto two bodily triads, one middle and one kaula.
uncertainties: kanda is rendered as bulb; its exact yogic referent can vary.
items.plain_english: The middle triad is said to be the middle of the brows, the throat, and the heart. The navel, the bulb, and the abode of great bliss form the kaula triad.

items.question: Where are all the named sacred sites ultimately located?
premises: Mountain tops, riverbanks, and solitary liṅgas were named as sacred places.
The text dismisses the need to multiply external examples.
All of them are said to be in consciousness and present in prāṇa.
items.inference: The entire outer sacred geography is ultimately internalized in consciousness and prāṇa.
items.plain_english: Mountain tops, riverbanks, and solitary liṅgas—why say more? All of that is in consciousness and present in prāṇa.
